growth_story.headline: Oil lifted Azerbaijan's income per person fast until 2007; since 2016, as output from ageing oil fields declines, growth has averaged 0.8 percent a year.
growth_story.arc: Income per person fell by 8.7 percent a year over 1991–1998, as the fall of the Soviet Union and the turmoil of the early 1990s brought a deep recession. From 1999 to 2007 it grew by 15.1 percent a year, the fastest era in the record, as oil production and exports from the Caspian rose during a global commodity boom; growth reached 33.0 percent in 2006. Growth slowed to 2.9 percent a year over 2008–2015 as the boom faded after the global financial crisis, and the 2014 fall in oil prices brought it to a halt. Since 2016 it has averaged 0.8 percent a year, against 8.0 in the decade before: income per person fell 4.1 percent in 2016 after two devaluations and a banking crisis, fell again in 2020, and output from mature oil fields keeps declining. In 2025 income per person reached its highest level so far, yet it grew only 1.0 percent that year.

threads.title: Public spending sets the pace
threads.text: In the oil years the state was a main investor, and its spending leaned toward public investment in infrastructure. That spending is now being cut back, and in 2026 lower government capital spending held down building work and investment.

threads.text: After a deep recession in the early 1990s, the country stabilised and put in place a production sharing agreement with a consortium of oil companies to develop its Caspian fields. Rising oil output and exports, during a global commodity boom, drove the very fast growth of 1999–2007.

threads.title: Oil price crash and devaluation
threads.text: Growth slowed after 2010, and the fall in oil prices in 2014 wiped out external surpluses. The central bank spent heavily to hold the exchange rate before the currency was devalued twice in 2015, and a credit crunch and banking crisis led into the 2016 recession.

since_last_year.text: Growth slowed sharply in the first half of 2026 as oil output kept falling and the government cut its capital spending. A spike in oil prices tied to conflict in the Middle East raised export earnings and the budget surplus, but not output. The IMF said in April 2026 that progress on a peace agreement with Armenia could support growth.

growth_story.tension: The sources date the slowdown from 2010 and treat 2008 as part of the oil boom, but the data place 2008 in the slower era even though income per person still grew 8.3 percent that year. The World Bank also calls 2016 the first recession since the turn of the century, while the data show income per person already fell in 2011 and 2015. Finally, the World Bank's average for total GDP growth over the past decade is above the 0.8 percent a year that income per person managed over 2016–2025, partly because the population grew.
